title: Pokémon Hits 30: How a Card-Catching Game Became the World's Biggest Franchise
summary:
Happy 30th birthday, Pikachu! Pokémon debuted on February 27, 1996, in Japan with just two video games. The goal was simple: catch and train fantastical creatures. Three decades later, it's the world's most valuable media franchise, according to Guinness World Records.

Millions of kids and adults now play Pokémon video games and apps, attend in-person events, and collect the mega-popular Pokémon Trading Card Game (TCG). The brand has celebrated all year with gatherings and new products, including a TCG expansion with glossy new cards.

From August 28 to 30, more than 50,000 fans crowded the Moscone Center in San Francisco, California, for the 2026 Pokémon World Championships. Some of the world's best players battled for hours in competitive TCG matches. TFK Kid Reporter Adam Sadi was on the scene and spoke with Haruki Okunishi, a top youth player who traveled from Malaysia. "I just practice and practice," Haruki told Adam, adding that all that practice is a lot of fun. Adam also got a lesson from a Pokémon Professor at the event on August 29.

So what's the secret to staying popular for 30 years? Barry Sams, vice president of game development and community engagement at the Pokémon Company International, told TIME for Kids that the brand does what Pokémon do best: it evolves. Sams says the company hopes to "keep moving forward." Part of that means making Pokémon more accessible. In 2025, the TCG became available in Latin American Spanish for the first time, and it's now in 16 languages.

Another championship attendee told Adam that Pokémon "brings together people of all backgrounds and all ages." Not bad for a game that started with two tiny cartridges.
why_it_matters: Pokémon shows how a hobby can grow into a worldwide industry and a community that spans languages and generations, so the way it adapts to new platforms and new fans is a live lesson in how brands, and fandoms, survive. For teenagers deciding what to spend time and money on, it is also a reminder that collecting and gaming are now global markets, not just playground trends.

background_read: Pokémon began in Japan as Pocket Monsters Red and Pocket Monsters Green — two slightly different versions of the same game, designed by Satoshi Tajiri (a game designer who collected insects as a child and turned that hobby into a game idea). Pikachu (the yellow, mouse-like creature that became the brand's mascot) was one of the 151 creatures in those first games.

Behind the brand sits The Pokémon Company International (the company, owned by Nintendo, Game Freak and Creatures, that manages Pokémon outside Japan), which licenses the games, cards, films and merchandise sold worldwide. Guinness World Records (a company that verifies and publishes record-breaking achievements, from the tallest human to the best-selling game) lists Pokémon as the highest-grossing media franchise, ahead of other entertainment giants.

The Trading Card Game grew out of the video games in the late 1990s and became a collecting hobby as well as a competitive sport; rare cards can now sell for far more than their original price. Pokémon Go (a phone game released in 2016 that uses GPS to place creatures in real-world locations) brought in millions of players who had never owned a handheld console.

perspectives.description: Thirty years of growth, 50,000 people at a single championship and a card game translated into 16 languages look like proof that Pokémon's 'evolve or fade' strategy works. For players, the community is the point: events bring together children, teenagers and adults who share one hobby.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — cost, hype and screen time
perspectives.description: Anniversary years come with new expansions and merchandise, and critics argue the constant release cycle pushes fans to keep buying and collecting. Some parents also worry about the money spent on rare cards and the hours poured into games and apps.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — how long-lived media brands survive
perspectives.description: Analysts point out that very few franchises last three decades, and the ones that do usually move from one medium to another: video games first, then cards, cartoons, films, phone apps and toys. Pokémon's longevity looks less like luck and more like a repeating pattern of re-releasing its core idea in new formats.

The open question is whether the next 30 years look like the last 30. Reaching new languages and regions may widen the audience, but digital play could also reduce interest in physical cards, and the brand will have to keep attracting players who were not born when Pikachu first appeared.
